slides.headline: Feel wobbly on one leg?
slides.sub: How Pilates trains balance through control, strength and awareness.

slides.title: Balance is a skill you can practise
slides.body: Balance relies on strength, your sense of where your body is, and how quickly you react. Like any skill, it tends to improve with regular, focused practice.

slides.title: Control through your middle
slides.body: Pilates builds strength and control through your trunk, hips and legs together. That steadier base can make it easier to stay upright when you shift your weight.

slides.title: Standing work on the reformer
slides.body: Standing and single-leg exercises on the reformer let you practise balance with support from springs and a hand on the bar. You can progress as you feel more confident.

slides.title: A simple move to try today
slides.body: Stand next to a kitchen bench and hold on lightly. Lift one foot and hold for 20 to 30 seconds. As it gets easier, use one finger, then none. Swap sides.

slides.title: Check with your GP or physio if
slides.body: You've had recent falls, feel dizzy or light-headed, or notice new numbness in your feet. These are worth a proper assessment before building a balance program.

slides.headline: Want to feel steadier on your feet?
slides.body: Our Pilates team at Hybrid Physiotherapy designs balance-focused programs that start where you are and build up gradually.

caption:
Can you stand on one leg for 30 seconds? It's a surprisingly useful check-in.

Balance relies on strength, body awareness and quick reactions, and like any skill it tends to improve with practice. Pilates builds control through your trunk, hips and legs together, and standing work on the reformer lets you practise with support from the springs and bar.

Try this today: hold a kitchen bench lightly and balance on one foot, then gradually reduce your grip. If you've had recent falls, feel dizzy or notice new numbness in your feet, check with your GP or physio first.
